newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Atlas Copco's drive into China not easy.
newsitem.headline: Atlas Copco's drive into China not easy.

text.p: Atlas Copco AB's drive into Asia is currently focused on China, but developing its Chinese business is no easy task with a lack of developed distribution channels, the Swedish engineering company said on Thursday.
"The paramount importance at this very moment is China and the wave coming after China," the company's chief executive officer designate Giulio Mazzalupi told Reuters in an interview.
Mazzalupi, who will replace Michael Treschow as president and CEO of Atlas at the end of April when Treschow moves to head Electrolux, is on a fact finding trip in Asia.
"You don't find partners that have a nationwide distribution and that is where we would be more interested to find partners," he said of China.
"What we are doing at the moment is to build our distribution ourselves and that is a big task. I believe that is the problem that most companies underestimate," he said.

Atlas Copco has five joint venture companies in China and has applied to Shanghai authorities to establish a holding company "that would be the financial vehicle and the mother of all our activity in China," said Mazzalupi.
Atlas Copco said annual turnover in the Asia/Australia region was about US$600 million, of which turnover in China was about US$70 million.
The group reported 1996 sales of 25.12 billion crowns ($3.3 billion) last month and profit after financial items of 3.07 billion crowns.

It said 1997 earnings were expected to increase somewhat over 1996 but noted that while demand was higher in North America, Southeast Asia, Australia and eastern Europe, sales developed negatively elsewhere in Europe.
"Our aim is to get a balance between the three macro regions of the world, the Americas, Europe and Asia," said Mazzalupi.
"We are balanced in America, we are over-represented in Europe and under-represented in Asia...The solution is to get Asia to grow faster," he said.
He said the company would also like to source more components which it uses in its products from Asia.

"Today we buy too much in Europe. We would like to buy more in this part of the world. This would give us a better trade balance with the region and on top of this a better currency balance and would create a better stability in our business."

Mazzalupi said the next area of growth would be Indochina and Indonesia. "There is a wave coming after China and basically it is Indochina and Indonesia. It is a big region that is going to develop," he said.

"Now we see countries like Vietnam, like Laos, like Cambodia - they are starting to appear on the scene and they are very eager to move towards industrialisation and building new infrastructure so for us it is very important," he said.
But he added: "In this part of the world what is most interesting is distribution but there are not many companies with already well-established distribution channels for our products."
